summary:
The legislative branch was the Congress. The 1971 Talisman calls it the Congress of Associated Students and records it as composed of a maximum of 43 members; the Herald called it the Associated Student Congress, and after 1972 the ASG Congress. The same volume gives its functions as establishing policies and programmes, ruling on petitions from student organisations seeking University recognition, and proposing modification of University policies affecting student activities and welfare, and describes an Executive Council of the four executive officers and three members elected from Congress, which considered policies and proposals before they went to Congress. Congress met weekly. Members were elected, the main offices in the spring, and Academic Council seats and freshman class offices in the autumn. In September 1974 the Herald reported that president Jeff Consolo named eight students to Congress seats; the archive does not record the rule under which he appointed them.

Congress rewrote its charter twice between 1970 and 1972. It endorsed a proposed constitution on 20 November 1970, and the Herald of 11 December 1970 reported that the constitution passed with 2,094 students voting, in the issue that also carried an editorial calling the referendum too much too late. A committee opened a fresh study of the constitutions in January 1971. The Constitution Revision Committee released its findings in September 1971, and the 1972 Talisman records that it presented President Dero Downing with guidelines for a new constitution that autumn. Congress voted on a section of the document on 22 February 1972, the Herald reported the executive branch accepted on 29 February, and the paper reported Congress approving the new constitution on 3 March 1972. A referendum followed on 29 and 30 March, and the Herald of 31 March reported that students had approved it. The 1973 Talisman sets out what the new constitution did: the body took the name Associated Student Government, the vice presidency was split into administrative and activities posts, and representation from the academic colleges replaced the special-interest groups previously represented, giving ten representatives at large, two from each academic college, the president and vice president of each class, and the ten Academic Council members and alternates. The archive holds no further charter work until March 1975, when the Herald reported a constitutional change approved.

Academic seats recur through the record. The Regents seated eight students on the Academic Council in August 1970. The 1973 Talisman states that 1972-73 was the first year Academic Council student members could vote on curriculum decisions; the 1972 Talisman, however, describes vice president Reginald Glass attending the Council in 1971-72 as one of two voting student members, and the archive does not resolve the conflict. For 1974-75, by president Jeff Consolo's account in the 1975 Talisman, there were two representatives from each of the University's seven colleges, half of them with voting status, out of 40 votes on the Council, and ASG drew up a resolution for the Council's Rules Committee asking for three more student votes, to make its three executive officers voting members.

Congress voted on 24 April 1973 to put a head fee increase to a student referendum; the 1974 Talisman records that the Regents instead approved an $11,000 increase in the student affairs budget allocated to ASG that August, which president Steve Yater said was better because it took no more money from students. ASG also set its own entertainment budget: the 1975 Talisman puts it at $42,000 for 1974-75, with $27,000 of that set aside for two free concerts. A bill seeking an ASG financial report was reported in the Herald of 18 October 1974, and Congress heard the treasurer explain the budget on 7 February 1975, in the issue that reported financial difficulties threatening ASG's entertainment role.

Quorum appears at both ends of the period. The Herald of 4 September 1970 reported that a failure to maintain a quorum had delayed action on key issues, and a quorum question tied to the Associated Student Congress constitution went on the ballot in October 1970. On 28 February 1975 the Herald reported ASG action halted twice that week for lack of a quorum. The archive carries nothing on quorum in the years between.

2. Invented rule. "the president filled vacancies by appointment" is inferred from the headline "Jeff Consolo Tabs Eight for Congress," which says neither vacancies nor appointment power. This is exactly the headline-as-article error.

3. False duration and implied continuity. "Congress spent five years rewriting its own charter" covers a rewrite that ran from 1970 to student ratification on 30 March 1972. The conflict must be printed beside the claim.

summary:
The legislative branch of Associated Student Government was called Congress. A congress member writing in ASG's own supplement said it met weekly to hold hearings, debate and conduct business; by 1978-79 it met each Tuesday in the Downing University Center. In 1975-76 ASG printed its own roll of 49 members in a supplement it paid for in the Herald. The roll gave five kinds of seat: eleven representatives-at-large; thirteen student members of the university's Academic Council; college representatives, two each from Applied Arts, the College of Education, Ogden and Potter and one each from the Community College, the College of Business and Public Affairs and the Graduate College; nine class officers; and the five executive officers, who sat as members. At-large and college seats were filled in an April election. In April 1976 the only contested college race was in business and public affairs; the Herald reported that all other college candidates were unopposed or the slots were not filed for, and that unopposed candidates would take office automatically.

Congress worked by bill and resolution. ASG's own list for 1975-76 numbered its bills 1 to 13 and noted that all passed unless marked otherwise; number 10 passed amended and number 13, a student evaluation of the administration, was tabled. The same supplement listed twenty-three resolutions and printed a result for each. Resolutions asked the university for things. Several bills governed ASG's own machinery: Bill 5 defined the structure of the committee system, Bill 7 defined how the treasurer could distribute funds, Bill 11 required a detailed monthly statement of expenditure published in the Herald, and Bill 12 created a temporary summer budget with final approval due by the third meeting of the fall semester. The money was not ASG's own. The treasurer worked with the other executive officers to formulate a budget, the Office of Student Affairs approved it, and student government received its funds from that office.

Discipline ran two ways. The secretary said in 1975-76 that a member was warned after four absences and removed after two more. As the Herald described the constitution in December 1978, a member was warned of possible dismissal after four absences and could be voted out of Congress after six, with the executive committee able to excuse absences for extenuating circumstances and the question going to Congress for a vote if it did not accept them. Removal by impeachment required the attendance of three-fourths of the full membership. Six congressmen moved on 16 March 1976 to investigate Gerard Faulk, chairman of the Judicial Council, over his handling of two cases sent to that council, one of them a misuse-of-funds charge brought against the treasurer. Congress acquitted him three weeks later: 28 members were present, no votes were cast in favour of removal, twelve were cast against and sixteen abstained, and for the second straight week the three-fourths attendance was missing. In the underlying case the Judicial Council had ruled in the treasurer's favour.

Constitutional revision ran the length of the block. A bill dated 7-14 September 1976 would have created a committee to revise the constitution; the record does not say whether it passed. Changes were still awaiting approval as the fall term opened in September 1977. Congress approved a revised constitution on 30 November 1978 and passed a constitutional amendment on 8 February 1979, and the Herald reported that students ratified the revision at the April 1979 general election, 1,343 to 170. The new constitution made 24 separate races for the 24 representative-at-large seats, which the administrative vice president said was meant to force competition between candidates, and changed the duties of the activities vice president to line up with the new University Center Board. By 1979-80 a constitutional amendment guaranteed eight on-campus, eight off-campus and eight general-representative seats on the congress in place of representation by 24 representatives at-large. Legislation surviving from that session carries year-prefixed numbering, as with Resolution 79-10 of 13 November 1979 on staffing for academic scholarships.

Funding moved the other way. After ASG lost more than $23,000 on major concerts, the dean of student affairs recommended halving its entertainment budget; on 29 April 1978 the regents let ASG keep its full $62,000 entertainment budget for 1978-79 and directed that a committee study who should control programming. On 31 March 1979 the regents approved a rebuilt University Center Board and funded it with $80,000 for programming, taking over from the autumn the lectures and concerts ASG had run. ASG's president, its activities vice president and one member of congress sat on the new board's committees.

What survives is the machinery and two uses of it: the Faulk impeachment, which failed for want of a three-quarters attendance, and the December 1978 case of activities vice president David Carwell, whose five absences put him one short of the six that allowed a removal vote. summary:
The legislative branch was the Student Congress. The constitution in force by 1985-86 vested in it all legislative authority of the Associated Student Government, the power to hear and approve the budget with recommendation for final approval by the university administration, to establish committees and agencies, to approve constitutional appointments by simple majority, and to function as a body in impeachment proceedings. Congress did not elect its own officers: ASG's five executive officers served as the officers of the Student Congress. The president presided over all regular and special meetings and was a non-voting member except to resolve a vote; the administrative vice-president, public relations vice-president, secretary and treasurer voted.

Membership was the president and vice-president of each of the four classes, one Academic Council representative and one alternate from each academic college, five on-campus, five off-campus and five at-large representatives, two freshman representatives elected each autumn, and the five executive officers. All but the freshman officers and representatives were elected in the spring, on dates the Rules and Elections Committee set at the new Congress's first meeting subject to Congress's approval. Representatives needed a 2.25 academic standing and, except for freshman class officers and representatives, one prior semester at Western; Academic Council representatives needed 2.75. Terms ran one academic year and began at least two weeks before the previous one ended. The amendment sheet bound with that constitution shows the design still moving: four freshman representatives instead of two, a delegate from every recognised student organisation, and vacancies filled after a two-week application period. What the corresponding documents said in 1980-81 has not been established here.

Congress met on Tuesdays, though not always; the meeting of 29 April 1982 fell on a Thursday. Legislation took two readings, normally a week apart, unless the rules were suspended, as they were on 6 May 1980, when a motion to suspend for Resolution 80-1 was defeated 20-8 with one abstention and a later suspension carried, and again on 9 April 1985. The Legislative Research Committee collected and reviewed every bill after its first reading, determined its constitutionality and researched conflicts with earlier legislation. Four recorded divisions survive from 1985-86, 26-4, 16-14, 4-28 and 7-14; the rest of the surviving measures passed unanimously or on a voice vote.

Seats went unfilled and members went absent. Under the constitution vacancies were filled by presidential appointment with the consent of a majority of Congress, and on 29 April 1982 Congress approved appointments to on-campus, off-campus, at-large and college seats in a single sitting, the new members sworn in by Judicial Council chairperson Gail Williams. At that meeting Treasurer Kelly Cook moved two by-law amendments on absence: one required a member absent from more than three meetings to appear before Congress and show cause why the seat should not be removed, after which Congress voted on removal; the other made one unexcused absence from a committee meeting equivalent to one unexcused absence from a Congress meeting. A bill requiring college representatives who missed two Academic Council meetings to come before the Judicial Council for possible dismissal was introduced on 8 April 1986 and passed unanimously on its second reading, 15 April 1986. A bill adopting a new application for open seats failed 7-14 on 1 April 1986, and a bill letting absent authors and sponsors vote by written approval filed with the recording secretary failed 4-28 after its first reading of 25 February 1986.

Congress legislated on residence-hall inspection, grading and withdrawal rules, campaign and election regulations, a book exchange and a student discount card, state education funding, and on its own machinery: abolishing the Finance Committee, creating a Financial Advisory Council, writing councils into the by-laws, opening college voting to every student's majors and minors, moving the Graduate College election to the autumn, and making the Kentucky Intercollegiate State Legislature a standing committee. Resolutions ran to 80-34 in 1980-81 and 81-13 in 1981-82, of which the archive holds 24 and all 13. In 1985-86 bills and resolutions shared one numbering sequence per semester, 17 numbers in the autumn and 39 in the spring, every one of which survives except 86-14-S.
problems:
Thirteen things must change before this is published under a university's name.

1. Wrong date of passage. "On 8 April 1986 a bill referring college representatives ... passed unanimously." 8 April was the introduction and first reading of Bill 86-31-S. The document reads First Reading 4/08/86, Second Reading 4/15/86, Pass Unanimously. It passed on 15 April 1986.

2. A date no source carries. "a bill letting absent authors vote by written proxy failed 4-28 on 4 March 1986." Bill 86-8-S records a first reading of 25 February 1986 and "Failed 4-28" with no date attached to the vote. 4 March 1986 appears in no cited source.

3. A number contradicted by the minutes. The summary says one 1982 amendment made "three unexcused committee absences equal to one unexcused Congress absence". The minutes of 29 April 1982 read that ONE unexcused absence from a committee meeting is equivalent to one unexcused absence from a Congress meeting.

4. A count the sources do not carry. "so between twenty and thirty-two members voted" is the writer's arithmetic on four tallies. Vote tallies count votes cast, not members present; abstentions and absences are not in them, and no source states a membership figure for 1985-86.

5. An absolute negative. "It elected no presiding officer of its own." The constitution says the executive officers served as officers of Congress; it nowhere says Congress elected none. Congress in fact appointed a parliamentarian and a sergeant-at-arms in April 1982.

6. Continuity across years the archive does not show. Every constitutional statement in the summary rests on one document, the constitution with amendments filed under a 1986 date, yet the summary presents it as the rule for 1980-81 through 1985-86. Worse, the amendments bound into that same document change what the summary states as settled: four freshman representatives rather than two, a new delegate seat for every recognised organisation, vacancies filled after a two-week application period rather than by presidential appointment, and five further constitutional committees.

7. A committee-chair error inherited from the fact list. The 29 April 1982 minutes name Jack Smith, not Kelly Smith, as Student Affairs chairperson. Kelly Smith was an on-campus representative appointed at the same meeting.

8. "Congress met on Tuesdays" is broadly right but stated flatly. The meeting the summary itself relies on, 29 April 1982, was a Thursday; the minutes refer to members "absent on Tuesday".

9. Two readings "a week apart" is stated as invariable. Bill 86-9-S records a second reading dated before its first, several forms leave a reading blank, and the rules were suspended to pass measures at first reading on 6 May 1980 and 9 April 1985.

10. An unsourced institutional claim. "With entertainment gone to the University Center Board" — nothing in the 45 facts says entertainment was transferred to the UCB. The UCB appears only as an organisation giving reports.

11. Topics with no source behind them. Of the legislative subjects listed, residence-hall inspection, grading and withdrawal rules, the book exchange, the discount card, state education funding and Congress's own machinery are all traceable. Visitation, library hours, lighting and crosswalks are not carried by any of the 45 facts.

12. A paragraph with no citation anywhere. "The secretary read openings from the chair: the Graduate College representative and alternate on 1 March 1983, and a representative-at-large as well a fortnight later." No fact in the list covers this and no URL is offered. The same applies to the absence counts for 1 March 1983, 15 March 1983 and 1 December 1981, which are attached to a URL that is the minutes of 2 April 1985.

13. Numbering presented as output. "It numbered thirty-four items in 1980-81" describes how far the series ran, not how much survives or how much passed; the archive holds 24 of those 34, and the 1980-81 series began on 6 May 1980, not in September. Also: "Fifteen seats were elected campus-wide" follows Article III Section 6 while Section 4 of the same constitution has on-campus representatives elected by students living on campus and off-campus representatives by students living off campus.

Two smaller points. The summary's "Seats came from four sources" omits the fifth: the five executive officers were themselves members of Congress. And the constitution's words are "a non-voting member of Congress except to resolve a vote"; "tie" is a gloss, defensible but not the text.

What is solid and should survive: the name and powers of Congress, the officers, the qualifications, the term dates, the Legislative Research Committee's role, and every one of the 1985-86 bills, whose vote tallies, reading dates and authors I confirmed against the page images (including "Passed 26 - 4" on Bill 85-2-F and "defeated 20-8, with 1 abstention" in the 6 May 1980 minutes).

summary:
Through these seven years the legislative branch was called Congress. Its own minutes use the term from 1993 on, and in September 2000 SGA's website still described Congress as the legislative body of SGA, charged with creating legislation. The rename from Associated Student Government to Student Government Association was proposed in Bill 92-10-S, a constitutional amendment dated 1 April 1992; the archive does not record how or when it took effect. The minutes that survive from October 1993, March 1994, February 1995 and September 1996 all record a 5 p.m. start on a Tuesday, and by September 2000 Congress met every Tuesday at 5 p.m. in Downing University Center 305. Each surviving set of minutes opens with a roll call, and names the absent.

Numbered legislation was the instrument. Every measure carried a code: two-digit calendar year, sequence number, and F or S for the semester, as Bill 93-1-F or Resolution 98-7-F. Bills and resolutions ran in separate sequences and both restarted each semester, so Bill 93-1-F, a set of constitutional amendments, and Resolution 93-1-F, on trash cans at shuttle stops, are different measures from the same session. A measure was introduced at a first reading and voted at a second, usually a week or two later; the printed cover sheet carried boxes for first reading, second reading, pass, fail and other, with the dates written in and the outcome marked. Congress could suspend its bylaws to take a measure in one sitting, as it did for Resolution 94-5-S on 29 March 1994. Bills allocated money, created programmes and amended the constitution and bylaws. Resolutions asked the university, its department heads or its Board of Regents for something.

Bill 93-1-F, Amendments to the Present Constitution, introduced 7 September 1993, proposed to rewrite who sat there. It provided twenty-four representatives at large drawn from off-campus and commuter students, eight each from the sophomore, junior and senior classes; five non-traditional representatives; five Academic Council representatives from each existing college, with an alternate for each college appointed by the president; residence hall representatives apportioned by hall population, one for a hall under 200 students rising to four for a hall of 600 or more; and a Freshman Council of eight. Everyone but the hall representatives and the Freshman Council was to be elected with the executive officers in the campus-wide election, on dates set by the Executive Council; those two groups were to be elected by the second Tuesday in September. Under the same document the vice president presided over Congress, could call a special meeting on twenty-four hours' notice, and voted only to break a tie. A revised constitution was in force by the following spring, when Bill 94-5-S of 29 March 1994 amended the bylaws to fit it, and by February 1995 vice president Tara Higdon was calling meetings to order.

Seats went unfilled, and the paper structure was never the real one. SGA's membership list for the autumn of 1994 names five executive officers and twenty-nine other members: six senior, eight junior and eight sophomore off-campus representatives, four college representatives, from Potter, Graduate, Ogden and Education, and three non-traditional representatives. It lists no residence hall representatives and no Freshman Council. On 28 February 1995 the secretary read twenty open positions into the minutes, nine of them elected seats and eleven of them single seats in named residence halls, and Congress voted three people into seats that night. The Herald's index records an article of 29 September 1994 headed "Student Government Association Officers Veto Homecoming Queen Idea", and another of 10 October 1996 on SGA proposing more lights and vetoing a resolution; the articles beneath those headlines are not readable in the digitised index, and the surviving minutes do not record either decision.

Volume varied by session. TopSCHOLAR and the archived SGA website together preserve 228 numbered measures from the fourteen sessions between the autumn of 1992 and the spring of 1999: 28 in 1992-93, 44 in 1993-94, 28 in 1994-95, 12 in 1995-96, 12 in 1996-97, 47 in 1997-98 and 57 in 1998-99. Fall 1993 produced eleven surviving bills and twenty resolutions; fall 1997 numbered resolutions to at least 97-25-F; fall 1998 preserves a complete run of thirteen bills, 98-1-F to 98-13-F; spring 1999 numbered bills to 99-23-S. The whole of 1996-97 survives only on the archived SGA website, and all twelve of its measures are from the spring; no legislation at all survives from the autumn of 1996, though that semester's minutes do.

Organizational Aid was disbursed by a numbered bill, with applicant organisations interviewed beforehand. Bills naming the recipients and the sums survive for spring 1993, fall 1993, spring 1994, spring 1995, fall 1997 and fall 1998, and again in fall 1999; none survives for 1995-96 or 1996-97. Bill 94-2-S divided $2,250 on 1 March 1994, Bill 95-2-S $2,500 on 7 March 1995, and Bill 98-9-F $6,200 on 27 October 1998, the same sum Bill 97-2-F had divided the year before. Congress also legislated on itself, with constitutional amendments in 1996 and a bill of March 1999 redefining the duties of the Coordinator of Committees. It ended the period defending its record: on 10 December 1998 vice president Matthew Bastin sent the advisor, the officers, the coordinator of committees, the committee heads and the Herald's editor a list of the autumn's passed legislation, written against accusations that SGA had been unproductive.
problems:
Nine problems, four of them numbers or dates the sources do not carry.

1. Invented count. "On 28 February 1995 the secretary read twenty-one open positions into the minutes." The minutes list twenty: two senior off-campus, two junior off-campus, four non-traditional and one graduate college seat, then eleven single hall seats (East, Florence Schneider, McLean, South, West, New Co-Ed, Sorority Hall, Bemis, Keen, Central, Barnes Campbell). The minutes never state a total, so the figure is the writer's own arithmetic, and it is off by one.

2. Wrong totals. "225 numbered measures" and the year-by-year figures behind it. Rebuilding the count the same way, from the whole TopSCHOLAR SGA collection unioned with the archived SGA website's 1997 and 1998 legislation indexes, gives 228, with 1995-96 at 12 rather than 10 and 1997-98 at 47 rather than 46. Five of the seven year figures are right.

3. Unsourced event. "Students had renamed the Associated Student Government the Student Government Association on the April 1992 ballot." Nothing cited, and nothing I could find, says a ballot was held or that it carried the rename. All the archive holds is Bill 92-10-S, a proposed constitutional amendment dated 1 April 1992.

4. Continuity where the archive is silent. "Organizational Aid ran through Congress every year." No disbursement bill survives for 1995-96 or for 1996-97, and the summary's own fact 21 skips both. The autumn 1995 bill it leans on, 95-1-F, is not a disbursement at all.

5. Overstated absence. "Nothing survives from the autumn of 1996." Only legislation is missing. Ten sets of minutes survive from August to December 1996, including the 17 September 1996 meeting the summary itself cites two paragraphs later for the Technology Committee.

6. An "only" claim that fails. Fact 24's "the one complete session" is repeated as "fall 1998 carried a complete run of thirteen bills". The bills are complete; the same session's resolutions are missing 98-3-F, and spring 1993 and spring 1994 run without a gap in both sequences.

7. A proposal described as the settled structure. Bill 93-1-F is presented flatly as what Congress was. It is a bill of amendments whose own text asks the administration to approve it, and the mirrored cover sheet has no reading dates or outcome marked. The fall 1994 roster then contradicts most of it: no hall representatives, no Freshman Council, four college representatives rather than five per college. What can be shown is that a revised constitution was in force by 29 March 1994, when Bill 94-5-S amended the bylaws to fit it, and that a single vice president was presiding by February 1995.

8. Two details drift from the documents. The constitution says five Academic Council representatives from each college, a number the summary drops; and it says elections are held with the executive officers on dates set by the Executive Council, not "in the spring campus-wide election".

9. Headline read as article, and a tidy dichotomy the facts break. The 1994 homecoming veto exists only as a headline in the Herald index, in Vol. 70 No. 11 rather than 70:12, and the article is not readable here; the claim that Congress had voted a week earlier is unsupported. Separately, "Bills spent money and created programmes" is contradicted by the summary's own centrepiece: Bill 93-1-F, Bill 96-2-S and Bill 99-14-S are all constitutional measures.

Minor, worth fixing while the file is open: "almost every dated bill and resolution is dated a Tuesday" should read most (198 of 242), and the 10 December 1998 memo was Bastin answering accusations that SGA had been unproductive, not a filing practice.

unanswered:
Not established, and stated plainly:

1. No quorum rule, attendance requirement or removal-for-absence rule for Congress was found anywhere in the block. Minutes record roll call and name the absent, but never a quorum count or a consequence. The nearest evidence sits outside the block: Bill 99-11-F, Committee Attendance Expectations (23 September 1999), and a "Fall Attendance Record" document catalogued to 2001. Whether an attendance rule existed 1992-99 is unknown.

2. Total seat count. The 1993 constitution fixes 24 at-large, 5 non-traditional and 8 Freshman Council seats, but leaves the college and residence hall totals dependent on how many colleges and halls existed and how large the halls were. No source found states a single number for the size of Congress in any year of the block. The fall 1994 roster (29 members) is a count of seats filled, not seats authorised.

3. What the amendments changed. The texts of Bill 92-14-S (31 March 1992), Bill 96-2-S (20 February 1996) and Bills 99-7-S, 99-8-S and 99-10-S (2 March 1999) could not be read: TopSCHOLAR's landing pages carry no abstract, and its PDF delivery returned bot challenges and then a 403 throughout this run. So the April 1996 ballot amendments, which the Herald covered twice, remain unexplained in substance. The same applies to Bill 99-16-S on congressional eligibility.

4. Numbering of sessions. No source found numbers successive congresses (no "the 30th Congress"). Sessions are identified only by calendar year and semester inside the legislation code. I have not claimed a numbering scheme that the record does not show.

5. Faculty Senate. Within this block SGA's academic resolutions ran to department heads and to the college Academic Councils, and the constitution seated the president on the Academic Council as a voting member. The earliest text found that addresses a body called the Faculty Senate by name is Resolution 00-2-S of 4 April 2000, which is outside the block. I have not projected that name backwards.

6. Autumn 1996 is blank. No numbered bill or resolution from the fall 1996 session survives in TopSCHOLAR, and the archived SGA website's legislation archive begins with 1997. The record is silent; it does not show that nothing was passed.

7. Session counts are floors, not totals. The 225 measures counted are the ones that survive. Gaps in the sequences are visible everywhere (fall 1994 has resolutions 94-3-F to 94-20-F with six numbers missing; fall 1997 bills survive as 1, 2, 3, 5). The highest surviving number in a session is the safest statement of how much that session carried.

8. Two cataloguing problems in the sources, flagged not fixed. (a) TopSCHOLAR lists both "Resolution 97-9-F - Paper Towels in Downing University Center Restrooms" and "Resolution 97-13-F - Papers Towels in Downing University Center Restrooms", while the SGA website's own 1997 index gives 97-13-F as the paper towels resolution and 97-9-F as lab assistants' knowledge of lab software. The existing years.json entry dated 1997-11-04 assigns paper towels to 97-9-F and cites a PDF filed as sga_res_94_9_f.pdf. Someone should check which number is right. (b) TopSCHOLAR also catalogues four fall 1997 resolutions with letters instead of numbers (97-F-A to 97-F-D) that appear to duplicate numbered items, and dates several undated items to 1 January.

9. Herald coverage is limited by two things. The digitised Herald issues are image PDFs with no text layer, so beyond the index headline nothing in an article is readable without OCR. And 5,061 of the 11,461 indexed items in data/herald-index-full.json have their index line truncated at exactly 300 characters, so any headline late in an issue's contents list is invisible to a grep. Articles such as "Student Government Association: Greeks Disproportional" (2 April 1996) and "Student Government Association: Proposal Expands" (16 November 1993), both plainly about the composition of the body, could not be read.

10. One observation offered to the editors, not a correction. Bill 93-1-F requires the president to take office at least two weeks before the end of the academic year and to assume all duties "except the position of Student Regent which shall be assumed on June 30." Read plainly, the 1993 constitution already treated the president as the holder of the Regent seat, and the archive's own 1994 Board of Regents entry describes Donald Smith as the previous SGA president and student regent. CLAUDE.md records the merger of the two offices as happening by about 2001. I have not changed anything; I note only that Bill 93-1-F is evidence worth weighing.

Method note: data/years.json was not edited and scripts/build.py was not run, as instructed. digitalcommons.wku.edu was left until last and requested one at a time with three-second gaps; landing pages and series indexes returned 200, but every PDF request returned a bot challenge or a 403, so no new PDFs were mirrored into the repository.

summary:
The legislative branch was called the Student Congress. SGA's own site said in September 2000 that Congress met every Tuesday at 5 p.m. in Downing University Center room 305, and its legislative branch page in January 2004 called Congress the one branch a student could join by filling out an application rather than by election or appointment, with an election held if applicants outnumbered seats. A member had to be enrolled full or part time, be in good standing and hold a 2.25 grade point average, and had to serve on at least one committee; the application form warned that after three absences the Judicial Council could terminate the seat.

The constitution as amended in spring 2001 gave Congress five non-traditional and five graduate representatives, ten representatives from each of the four classes, residence hall seats apportioned from one to four by hall population, ten at-large seats, an Academic Council representative and an alternate for each college, and the Coordinator of Committees and every standing and ad hoc committee chair as presidential appointments. Amendment 3 replaced that clause with two graduate representatives, two from each class, the same hall apportionment, ten at-large places, five off-campus places and two from each academic college, with the same appointed positions; academic college representatives needed a declared major, a 2.75 overall grade point average and a 3.0 in the major. The date Amendment 3 was ratified is not established, and SGA's site was still posting the Spring 2001 text with six appended amendments in January 2004. Sophomore, junior and senior class seats were filled in spring elections and the remaining elected seats in the fall; members took office by the second week of September and served the rest of the academic year. Congress approved the budget for the university's final approval, sat as a judicial body in impeachments, could override a veto by a two-thirds vote, and amended the constitution by a two-thirds vote of its full membership followed by ratification in a student referendum, with the Judicial Council reviewing amendments first.

The constitutional committees were the Committee on Committees, which only Congress members could join, and Legislative Research, Student Affairs, Academic Affairs, Public Relations and Campus Improvements, all open to any student, each with a chair appointed by the president and approved by a majority of Congress. SGA's own site also listed Hillraisers and Special Events among its committees in 2000, a Senior Banquet committee in 2001, and an ad hoc Organizational Aid Committee in 2003-04. Legislation was numbered by semester and marked bill or resolution, was sponsored by committees, and went to the Legislative Research Committee before its second reading. SGA's legislation archive holds nothing for 1999, 2000, 2001 or spring 2002; it lists twenty pieces for fall 2002, thirteen for spring 2003, twenty for fall 2003 and twelve for spring 2004. The Herald reported on 29 April 2003 that the year had closed after more than 55 pieces of legislation.

Attendance was a running problem. The Herald of 20 April 2000 carried an item headlined for still-declining SGA membership. At the fourteenth meeting of the year, on 2 December 2003, 25 of 43 members were present.

Bill 03-10-F, a new constitution and bylaws written by Legislative Research Committee chair Robert Watkins, was entered in SGA's legislation archive on 10 November 2003, and the minutes record that it passed with general consent on 2 December 2003. It renamed Congress the Senate and set 35 seats: four from each of the four classes, two graduate representatives and seventeen at-large. It created a Speaker of the Senate, elected from the elected Senate by the previous semester's legislative branch, who presided, served as Coordinator of Committees and appointed a Secretary of the Senate subject to Senate approval. It lowered the seat requirement to a 2.0 grade point average and full-time enrolment, raised the veto override to three-fourths, and left vacancies after the fall elections to presidential appointment with majority Senate approval. The accompanying bylaws set a simple-majority quorum, allowed four absences a semester unless excused, required committee service of every senator but the Speaker and the University Senate representatives, and were to take effect for fall 2004.

The Herald reported that the vice presidency of finance was folded into administration, that public relations became an appointed post, that the branch would shrink from 75 to 35 and be elected by students where empty seats had previously been filled by appointment, and that the executive branch could no longer present legislation to the senate. On 22 January 2004 it reported that no vote had yet been taken because two-thirds of the body had not been present at the previous two meetings, and that President John Bradley said all 75 positions had never been filled during his time in SGA. On 16 March it reported that approval by the legislative branch had taken five attempts for want of attendance, and that students ratified the constitution in a referendum on 9 March 2004. The election codes adopted on 22 January 2004 set internet polling from 16 to 17 March 2004, and the Herald of 18 March reported that 1,232 students voted and that the first senate under the new constitution was chosen at the same time. On 15 April 2004 the Herald reported that Watkins had been elected the first speaker of the senate by 9 votes to 8 over Brittany Fausey, 17 of the 20 members present voting, and that the result was questioned at once because the new constitution was unclear whether two-thirds of eligible voters or of total membership was required and because three members present had been barred from voting under a judicial council ruling. Fausey did not challenge the result.
problems:
The 32 facts are in good shape: 28 are supported as written, 4 need their sourcing corrected, none is contradicted or unreachable. The summary is not. It carries at least a dozen numbers, dates and claims the facts do not support, and one plain misreading.

1. "In 2002-03 the body heard more than 55 pieces of legislation." No cited fact carries this. SGA's own archive lists 20 items for fall 2002 and 13 for spring 2003, 33 in all, 42 even if you assume every skipped number was a real bill. The figure is real but comes from elsewhere: the Herald of 29 April 2003, already cited in this repository at data/years.json (https://wkuherald.com/56877/news/sga-brings-year-to-end/). Cite it or drop it.

2. "Membership reached 71 in September 2002." No source anywhere. The Wayback Machine captured only the 2002-03 minutes index, never the individual meeting PDFs, so no roll count for that autumn survives in the cited record. Delete it.

3. "By 13 April 2004 there were 20 members." This misreads the speaker-vote report. The Herald of 15 April 2004, cited in data/years.json, says 17 of the 20 members present voted. Twenty present at one meeting is not a membership of twenty.

4. "Watkins was elected the first Speaker on 13 April 2004 by 9 votes to 8." The 9-8 count is right and the loser was Brittany Fausey, but the date 13 April is an unsourced inference from the Tuesday meeting pattern; the source is a report of 15 April. Worse, the summary presents a clean result. The same report says the outcome was immediately questioned because the new constitution was unclear whether two-thirds of eligible voters or of total membership was needed, and three members present had been barred from voting by a judicial council ruling. A disputed election reported as a tidy 9-8 is the kind of smoothing this archive cannot publish.

5. "The Herald reported on 12 February 2004 that Congress had approved the constitution and bylaws unanimously on its fifth attempt ... and that the Judicial Council had struck about 13 members from the roll." There is no 12 February source in the fact list. The five-attempts detail exists, but in the 16 March 2004 article (fact 30's source), which says approval took five attempts because there were not enough members present. That article does not say the vote was unanimous, and nothing in any cited source says the Judicial Council struck about 13 members for missing more than three meetings. Two invented specifics attached to a phantom citation.

6. "Students ratified it in an online referendum on TopNet on 9 March 2004 by 116 votes to 16, out of 132 cast." The 9 March referendum and its passage are in the 16 March article. The 116-16 split is in no cited source, and "on TopNet" is in none either: the election codes describe internet polling run with Information Technology. The only vote figure in the record I could reach is the Herald editorial of 16 March 2004 noting 132 of about 18,000 students voted.

7. "The first Senate was elected on 16 and 17 March 2004." Fact 17 is an election code setting those polling dates, and the 16 March article says the senate will be elected today and tomorrow. That is a schedule and an advance notice, not a result. The result is in the Herald of 18 March 2004, already in data/years.json: 1,232 students voted.

8. "The Herald reported declining membership in April 2000." Uncited, and what survives in data/herald-index-full.json is an index line, that is, a headline: "Hall, Rex. Student Government Association Membership Still Declining," Herald 75:54, 20 April 2000. Reporting the headline as the article is exactly the failure this project spent a day removing.

9. "The constitution allowed 75 seats." The constitution states no total and cannot, because residence hall seats vary with hall population. 75 is the Herald's figure for elected legislative members, and it belongs with Bradley's remark that all 75 had never been filled.

10. The seat structure is described as one fixed arrangement for all five years. The classes listed (graduate, four classes, halls, at-large, off-campus, colleges) are Amendment 3's, and fact 7 explicitly says the ratification date was not established. The clause it replaced had five non-traditional and five graduate representatives, ten per class, no off-campus seats and Academic Council rather than academic college seats. As written the paragraph is wrong for 1999-2000 and probably for 2000-01 and 2001-02.

11. "Made every seat elective." Contradicted twice over. Fact 27: vacancies after the fall elections are filled by presidential appointment with Senate approval. Fact 30's article: the legislative branch was required to be elected under the old constitution too, and what changed is that empty seats were no longer filled by appointment. The Speaker also appoints the Secretary, and under the bylaws nominates every committee chair.

12. Meeting time and room rest on a single capture of 2 September 2000, and the application route on a capture of 6 January 2004. Both are stated flatly for 1999-2004. The proposed bylaws put the Senate in the Senate Chambers, so even the room did not hold.

13. The committee list omits the Committee on Committees, which fact 12 makes constitutional and fact 15 shows operating in 2003-04, and it hides the fact that SGA's own site listed Hillraisers and Special Events in 2000 and a Senior Banquet committee in 2001, and an ad hoc Organizational Aid Committee in 2003-04.

14. "Bills and resolutions ... took two readings and were sponsored by committees." True for the period, but the fact list sources it to the proposed bylaws of fall 2003, which by their own ratification clause took effect for fall 2004. The standing constitution supports it directly: the Legislative Research Committee reviewed all legislation before its second reading, and the veto clause names the sponsoring committee.

15. "Congress passed it by general consent on 2 December 2003" is correct and I confirmed it in the minutes, but it is not in the fact list, and the summary sets it beside a February approval without reconciling either with the Herald of 22 January 2004, which reported the constitution still needed a second reading and a vote and that no vote had been possible because two-thirds of the body had not attended the previous two meetings. The sequence is genuinely awkward and must be stated, not smoothed.

16. Watkins's authorship and the two executive changes (finance folded into administration, public relations made appointive) are true and I verified them, but no listed fact carries them; they come from the Herald of 22 January and 16 March 2004 and the 2 December minutes.

The minutes record the bill passing with 25 of 43 members present, below two-thirds of the full membership; the Herald of 12 February 2004 records approval on a fifth attempt after earlier failures for want of two-thirds present. summary:
The constitution proposed in the autumn of 2003 and put to students the following spring named the legislative branch the Student Senate. The body it replaced had been called Congress, and the new text still slipped into the old name twice, at 3.4.4 and 3.10.4. The Senate had thirty-five seats: four senators from each of the four class years, two graduate senators and seventeen at large. Its list of seats was exhaustive, and it reserved none for a residence hall, an academic college or off-campus students, all of which the constitution it replaced had provided for. Twenty-eight seats were filled at the spring election and seven, the four freshman seats and three at large, in the autumn, and graduate seats left empty in the spring became at-large seats in the autumn. Senators elected in the spring took office no sooner than two weeks after the fall term began, those elected in the autumn no sooner than two weeks after that election, and both served one academic year. A Senate seat required a 2.0 cumulative grade point average, good standing and full-time enrolment. The amendments proposed in the spring of 2005 raised that to 2.5.

The Senate elected a Speaker from among its own elected members, by a vote of the previous semester's legislative branch. The Speaker presided, served as Coordinator of Committees, appointed the Secretary of the Senate subject to the Senate's approval, called special meetings on twenty-four hours' notice, and reported excessive absences to the Judicial Council. Five standing committees, Legislative Research, Student Affairs, Academic Affairs, Public Relations and Campus Improvements, were written into the constitution as part of the legislative branch and were open to any student who wished to serve. The 2004 constitution put their chairs in the Speaker's gift. The 2005 amendments moved that appointment to the President, and added a vote of no confidence in the Speaker and a procedure for removing a committee head, neither of which the 2004 text had. The bylaws of the same season did not follow: they still gave the chairs to the Speaker, and the two governing documents remained in conflict on the point.

Under the 2004 bylaws the Senate met at 5 p.m. every Tuesday of the academic year in the Senate Chambers unless a majority agreed otherwise, and a simple majority of the membership was a quorum. By November 2009 SGA's website was giving the room as DUC 305. Legislation needed a committee sponsor, took two readings, and went to the Legislative Research Committee in between with an author present. Once passed, the Executive Cabinet had fourteen days to ratify or reject it, and silence counted as approval. The two documents disagreed on what it took to override a veto: the constitution said three-fourths of the Senate, the bylaws two-thirds of those present and voting, and the bylaws cited the constitution for the figure they contradicted. The 2005 amendments brought the constitution down to two-thirds. The Senate also approved the budget, confirmed constitutional appointments, wrote its own bylaws and election code, and sat as the trial body in impeachments, which took the written endorsement of a fifth of the membership to begin, a special session under the Chief Justice, at least fourteen days before a final vote, and two-thirds of the full membership to carry.

Elections were run by the Judicial Council under codes it enacted subject to a majority vote of the Senate. The codes adopted in January 2004 capped spending by a candidate for the legislature at $50, against $450 for a candidate for president, and set internet polling for 16 and 17 March 2004.

Filling the chamber was another matter. The autumn of 2009 is the stretch the archive documents best: the roll ran 23 on 8 September, 24 on 15 September and 32 on 22 September, once the judicial council had certified the fall election. On 29 September the minutes put it at 36, one seat more than the constitution allowed. It stood at 32 through October, then at 30 on 27 October, after three senators resigned on the floor on 20 October and a fourth on 27 October. SGA's website that November listed twenty-nine people on the legislative side: twenty-seven student senators, the Speaker and the Secretary of the Senate.

SGA numbered its own bodies in its minutes. The senate that opened on 5 September 2006 called itself the first meeting of the fifth Student Government Association, and was still the fifth senate that December. The 2009-10 senate called itself the eighth Senate in every set of its minutes examined here, from September 2009 through April 2010. Its legislation numbering had reversed along the way: spring 2004 bills ran year first, as in B 04-1-S, while by the autumn of 2006 the sequence came first, as in Bill 11-06-F, and it still did in Bill 30-10-S in April 2010. No document found dates the change.
problems:
The governing-document work is genuinely good. Facts 2 through 3, 5 through 17 and 19 through 23 are exact against the primary texts, and the two constitutional contradictions the page finds, the three-fourths against two-thirds override and the committee-chair conflict between the 2005 constitution and the 2005 bylaws, both hold up. The prose summary is a different matter. It carries a large body of numbers that the thirty-one facts do not support, and two errors of substance.

Numbers, dates and counts in the summary with no numbered fact behind them:
1. "ratified a new constitution on 9 March 2004 by 116 votes to 16". No fact carries either the date or the tally. The only cited document that touches the date is the election codes calendar, which lists "March 9: Vote on new Constitution (Tentative)". The archive elsewhere holds a Herald editorial of 16 March 2004 reporting 132 of about 18,000 students voting, and 116 plus 16 is 132, so the tally is probably right, but it needs its own numbered fact and source before it can be printed as a flat statement.
2. "fell from 75 seats to 35". Nothing gives 75. I opened the pre-2004 constitution, which is the document that would have to say so, and it does not: its Congress was part fixed and part variable, with residence hall seats apportioned by hall population, so it has no single total on its face. Either source 75 or drop it.
3. "the seats that had belonged to residence halls, academic colleges and off-campus students were abolished". True, and provable from the pre-2004 constitution, arts. 3.3.4, 3.3.6 and Amendment 3 at 1.1.5, but no cited fact establishes what the earlier body contained. Fact 2 only says the 2004 Senate reserved none.
4. "Congress became the Student Senate". Same gap as fact 1. Provable, unsourced as filed.
5. The whole seat-filling paragraph. "Nine students filed for the 28 spring seats in March 2004", "Congress had 20 members when it elected the first Speaker that April", "Twenty-three seats were filled in September 2004", "twenty-five candidates ran unopposed in March 2005", "opened 2006-07 with eighteen", "reached 31 by November 2006", "lost quorum on 5 December with 16 present", "Twenty-five students ran for 20 seats in autumn 2007", "nine were seated in autumn 2008", "the roll stood at 32 in October 2009 and 30 in February 2010". Not one of these is in the thirty-one facts. Several are real, and I confirmed four of them directly from documents already in this repository during this review: 8 of 18 senators on 5 September 2006, 22 of 31 on 28 November 2006, 16 of 31 on 5 December 2006, and the autumn 2009 rolls. The rest, including "nine were seated in autumn 2008" and "30 in February 2010", I could not confirm at all. A paragraph that is ten numbers long and zero facts deep is exactly how twenty-two errors got onto the last page.
6. "the amendments ratified in March 2005" and "Their chairs were appointed by the Speaker until March 2005". The facts say spring 2005, and the documents are headed "As Proposed Spring 2005". March is an added month.
7. "the 2006-07 senate called itself the fifth Student Government Association". Correct, and fact 24 carries it, but the summary's phrase "SGA's own minutes numbered the bodies" then implies a continuous practice across the six years, which only two of the six are shown to have.

Errors of substance carried up from the facts:
8. The summary inherits nothing from fact 4, which is good, because fact 4 reverses the constitution. But it does inherit fact 30's miscount indirectly by tone. Fix fact 30: the November 2009 page lists twenty-nine people in all, not twenty-nine senators plus two officers.
9. "Their chairs were appointed by the Speaker until March 2005, when the amended constitution moved that appointment to the President" is too clean. The page's own fact 23 shows the bylaws of the same season kept the appointment with the Speaker, so the two governing documents disagreed on the point for years. The summary should not tidy away a conflict the facts went to the trouble of finding.
10. "The Senate met at 5 p.m. every Tuesday in the Senate Chambers" is stated as a constant for the whole period, sourced only to the 2004 bylaws. By November 2009 SGA's own site said DUC 305, per fact 30. That is the archive having no record of continuity in between.
11. "Seats went unfilled from the start" characterises rather than describes, and the sentence exists only to introduce the unsourced number paragraph.
12. The penultimate paragraph, "organizational aid, textbook and study-abroad scholarships, benches, bike racks, recycling bins and extended library hours by bill; printing quotas, plus/minus grading, state funding and the move to Division I-A football by resolution", is supported by nothing in the thirty-one facts. Most of it is in years.json with sources attached, but as filed here it is an eleven-item list with no citation at all.

Two smaller notes for the editor. The 15 September 2009 minutes file misdates its own header to September 8, and the file named april20.doc heads itself 13 April 2010; both should be described by what the document says, not by the file name. And the roll of 36 senators recorded on 29 September 2009, one above the constitutional maximum of 35, is a better fact than most of what the seat-filling paragraph currently carries, and it is sitting unused.

summary:
The legislative branch was the Student Senate. Its constitution made it the official voice of the student body, gave it the power to establish bylaws, had it approve the budget with recommendation for final approval by the university administration, and let it override an Executive Cabinet veto by a two-thirds vote. Under the bylaws it met at 5 p.m. every Tuesday of the academic year in the Senate Chambers unless it agreed otherwise. Sittings were numbered by session and by meeting: the sixteenth Senate sat in 2017-18, the twenty-fourth in 2024-25, and the twenty-fifth in 2025-26, whose twenty-sixth meeting fell on 14 April 2026.

The constitution in force for 2017-18 listed 36 seats: three each for the senior, junior, sophomore and freshman classes, two graduate, one English as a Second Language International, one Gatton Academy, one from each of six academic colleges, and fourteen at large. Bill 12-21-S, first read 2 March 2021, moved the academic-college senators, the international senator and three at-large seats from the fall election to the spring, leaving three freshman, one graduate and one Gatton Academy seat to the fall, with any unfilled fall seat becoming an at-large seat in the same election. By 2023 the constitution counted five academic-college senators, and Bill 13-23-F, read on 14 and 28 November 2023, took that back to six by adding a Mahurin Honors College senator. The constitution now posted lists 38 seats: one graduate senator rather than two, the international senator returned to the fall election, and new seats for transfer and non-traditional students, the Intercultural Student Engagement Center and first-generation students.

Committees were rebuilt mid-decade. The 2017-18 constitution named eight: Legislative Research, Student Affairs, Academic Affairs, Public Relations, Campus Improvements, Diversity and Inclusion, Sustainability and SAVES, their heads appointed by the President with the approval of a majority of the Senate. Most of those names, together with an Organizational Aid Committee, were still sponsoring legislation in spring 2021. From the fall of 2021 the sponsors named in the archive are Legislative Operations, Enrollment and Student Experience, Outreach and Student Experience, Campus Improvements, Diversity Equity and Inclusion, and Student Mental Health and Wellbeing. Bill 21-22-S, read on 8 and 22 March 2022, proposed a Community Relations Committee to advocate for students' needs in Bowling Green and encourage civic involvement rather than a political agenda; the archive records the bill as tabled, and the committee first appears as a sponsor in October 2022. Bill 4-22-F, passed 36-1 on 11 October 2022, renamed three of the committees. Bill 32-24-S, first read 12 March 2024, moved the appointment of committee heads from the President to the Speaker, still subject to a two-thirds vote of the Senate. The constitution now posted lists seven standing committees, ending with Action & Opportunity and Community Relations, and by 2025-26 the archive also shows a Campus Safety and Security Committee and a Bylaws Review Committee sponsoring legislation.

SGA is given $100,000 each school year. The Executive Cabinet drafts the budget, the Senate approves it, and the university administration gives final approval. The 2024-25 budget included $20,000 for organizational aid, $23,500 for scholarships and $10,705 in legislative discretionary funding, and passed at the first meeting of the 24th Senate on 27 August 2024. The bylaws require that the Legislative Discretionary Fund never fall below a tenth of the total budget as proposed by the Chief Financial Officer. At the twenty-sixth meeting of the 25th Senate, on 14 April 2026, the Chief Financial Officer reported $71.17 remaining, and the last two bills of the night were amended to spend it.

The rules for membership tightened in the same decade. Bill 29-24-S raised the minimum cumulative grade point average to 2.75 for executive officers and 2.5 for senators; Bill 26-24-S directed the removal of any member censured twice in one academic year; Bill 22-24-S changed the threshold for a constitutional amendment from two-thirds of the full Senate membership to two-thirds of those present; Bill 23-24-S moved amendment referendums into the fall and spring senator elections. The bylaws adopted 24 February 2026 allowed no more than two unexcused Senate absences a semester before the Speaker referred a member to the Judicial Council.

The recorded disputes turned on money, on Greek life, and on who controlled the Senate's own business. In August 2017 the Senate rejected Bill 5-17-F, which would have barred the executive branch from writing legislation, by 4-8, and in November 2017 Bill 32-17-F, which would have removed the first reading, failed. In October 2018 Bill 10-18-F, which would have barred SGA funding to Interfraternity Council and Panhellenic Council chapters, was defeated 16-17. In March 2024 Bill 32-24-S took the appointment of committee heads from the President and gave it to the Speaker.

Legislation was numbered N-YY-F in the fall and N-YY-S in the spring. The spring series began again at one in most sessions, though in 2022-23 it continued the fall numbering. SGA publishes the record on two web pages, one covering Fall 2011 to Spring 2025 and one covering Fall 2025 to Spring 2026, each session in its own table giving the item's title linked to its file, its number, authors, sponsoring committee, both reading dates and whether the Senate and the Executive Cabinet passed it, with some of those fields left blank. The tables list 71 items for 2017-18, 55 for 2018-19, 16 for 2019-20, 30 for 2020-21, 56 for 2021-22, 54 for 2022-23, 54 for 2023-24, 48 for 2024-25 and 60 for 2025-26.

The summary carries at least fifteen defects, several of them contradicted by the very documents cited.

1. "its last sitting, on 14 April 2026" - the cited minutes refer to a later meeting twice (office hours due by the 28 April meeting; the Secretary cannot attend "the last meeting / the swearing in of the new senate"). Only the Herald calls 14 April the final meeting.

2. "The 2025-26 Senate finished with $71.17 of it left" - no supplied fact carries this number, and it is backwards. The 14 April minutes show the CFO reporting $71.17 left and the last two bills passing; the Herald of 14 Apr 2026 says those two bills were amended to use up the remaining $71.17. The Senate spent it, it did not finish with it.

3. "leaving three freshman, one graduate, one international and one Gatton Academy seat to the fall" - contradicts fact 6. Bill 12-21-S moved the international senator INTO the spring; its revised s3.7.1 leaves only freshman, graduate and Gatton seats in the fall. The international senator is back in the fall in the constitution now posted (s3.9.1), which is a later change the summary silently folds into 2021.

4. "Bill 13-23-F added a Mahurin Honors College senator in November 2023, taking the total to 38" - the bill only changes academic-college senators from five to six. The 38 comes from the later constitution, which also carries the transfer/non-traditional, ISEC and first-generation seats. Worse, the summary has already told the reader the 2017-18 constitution had six college seats, so a bill adding a sixth reads as an error unless the drop from six to five in between is stated.

5. "Bill 21-22-S added a seventh, Community Relations, on 22 March 2022" - the archive records 21-22-S as Tabled at both the Senate and Executive stages, the bill's own Pass/Fail lines are blank, and a constitutional amendment needs a student referendum besides. The committee first appears as a sponsor in October 2022. No source states a total of seven at that date.

6. "Bill 31-24-S made Outreach the Outreach and Public Relations Committee in 2024" - not among the thirty facts and uncited. I checked it independently and it is true (first read 12 March 2024, at .../2023_2024_legislative/legislation/bill_31_24_s.pdf), but the PDF's own header misnumbers itself "Bill 31-24-F", which a reader will notice. Cite it or drop it.

7. "the Diversity, Equity and Inclusion Committee became the Action and Opportunity Committee by student referendum in April 2025" - not among the facts and uncited. It is supported by data/years.json (Senate passed Bill 21-25-S on 4 April 2025; the student body ratified it on 16 April with 88 per cent, Herald 16 Apr 2025). Note also that the archive labels items from October 2024 onward as sponsored by the Action and Opportunity Committee, apparently relabelled retroactively, so do not write that the name first appears in 2025.

8. "The seven were renamed but not replaced after that" - a continuity claim the archive does not carry. In 2025-26 the sponsor column shows a Campus Safety and Security Committee, a Bylaws Review Committee and an Organizational Aid Board, and the 14 April 2026 minutes report a combined "Student Mental Health and Wellbeing / Campus Safety and Security".

9. "A session spent $100,000" - the source says SGA is given $100,000 each school year. Nothing shows a session spending all of it; the Herald in fact quotes the CFO setting that as a goal. Likewise "its constitution ... gave it the budget" overstates s3.1.3, which has the Senate approve the budget with recommendation for final approval by the university administration, on a draft written by the Executive Cabinet.

10. "In 2024-25 that was $20,000 ... $23,500 ... $10,705" - the Herald says the budget "includes" those three lines plus office supplies, public relations and project funds. Write "included", not "that was".

11. "in the Senate chambers of the Downing Student Union" - the bylaws say only "the Senate Chambers". DSU is supported by data/years.json (fall election results announced in the Senate Chamber of Downing Student Union), but the sentence as written has no source behind the location.

12. "Senators tried and failed to bar the executive from writing legislation and to abolish the first reading in 2017, and to defund Greek chapters in 2018" - none of this is in the thirty facts. All three are real and are in data/years.json with Herald citations: Bill 5-17-F failed 4-8 (Herald 31 Aug 2017); Bill 32-17-F failed for want of a motion (Herald 30 Nov 2017; the archive records it No / No); Bill 10-18-F was defeated 16-17 (Herald 17 Oct 2018). The last was a bar on SGA funding to Interfraternity Council and Panhellenic Council chapters, not "defunding Greek chapters", which reads as cutting off the chapters themselves.

13. "The recurring fights were over money, Greek life, attendance, who controlled the Senate, and whether a nonpartisan body should speak on national questions" - an unsourced characterisation of a decade. Replace with the specific documented episodes and their outcomes.

14. "restarted each semester" - true of most sessions but not all: in 2022-23 the spring series continued the fall numbering (fall ran to 26-22-F, spring ran 27-23-S to 41-23-S).

15. "Each item carried both reading dates on its face, a purpose clause, numbered whereas clauses, named authors and a sponsoring committee" - contradicted by the cited bills themselves. Bill 2-21-F has a blank second reading and no sponsor; bills 12-21-S, 21-22-S, 1-22-F and 4-22-F have unnumbered whereas clauses (only the 2023-24 bills number them).

16. "SGA published every item since 2011 in a table on its own website" - it is two pages carrying about sixteen tables, the 2025-26 items are on a second page the citation never reaches, "every item" is not verifiable from the tables, and many rows leave the sponsor, second reading or pass columns blank.

17. Smaller: "By the fall of 2021 six new ones did ... Campus Improvements and Sustainability" - the fall 2021 sponsor column reads "Campus Improvements Committee"; the "and Sustainability" name appears from spring 2022. And fact 4's committee list for 2019-20 is wrong (Sustainability sponsored nothing that session; Organizational Aid sponsored four items), so any sentence resting on it must change too.
