summary:
The judicial branch of WKU student government was the Judicial Council. The constitution as amended in spring 2001 vested the association's judicial authority in it and named it one of three branches alongside Congress and the executive. The 2000 Election Codes, citing Article IV, Section 5, opened by stating that the council supervised all elections.

Under the 2001 constitution the council had five justices. The president appointed them and Congress confirmed them, by a majority vote under the amendment package Bill 93-1-F, introduced on 7 September 1993, and by a two-thirds vote under the 2001 text. The president named one of the five as chief justice, subject to a majority vote of Congress. Justices served one academic year and took office no later than two weeks after the fall term began. They had to have been enrolled at Western for the year before appointment, hold a 2.5 cumulative grade point average, stay enrolled and in good standing, and not sit in Congress at the same time. Vacancies were filled within two weeks, and the council's records were posted for two weeks before being filed in the SGA office. The 2001 constitution had the chief justice schedule bi-weekly meetings; the bylaws proposed in spring 2002 required the council to meet at least twice a month in the SGA offices, and to comply with the Kentucky Open Meetings Law.

Its powers were listed. It interpreted the constitution and bylaws on request. It held judicial review over the acts of Congress, at the request of any registered student. It heard all appeals about elections and candidates' qualifications. It wrote the election rules, subject to a majority vote of Congress. It reviewed constitutional amendments before Congress voted on them. It could exempt an executive candidate from the requirement of a year's prior membership in Congress, a power that Amendment 4 later removed when it fixed service requirements for each office and barred exemptions. The chief justice swore in the officers and members of Congress and presided over impeachments of executive and legislative officers; a justice's own impeachment was presided over by a member of Congress instead. Under the spring 2002 bylaws the council also handled attendance: Congress members were allowed three absences a semester, with no distinction between excused and unexcused, and a member with four or more was referred to the council, had to appear and explain, and had an answer within seven days. A justice with two unexcused absences was subject to impeachment.

The election codes dated 7 March 2000 set out the routine: a compulsory candidates' orientation meeting fourteen days before the primary, a random draw for ballot position, polling places in Margie Helm Library, the Preston Center and Downing University Center from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., itemised campaign finance reports filed with the council, and the count, which the chief justice opened by unlocking the ballot boxes. Spending was capped at $750 for a president and vice president ticket, $400 for other executive candidates and $50 for a Congress seat, with no donor giving more than $100. Ballots were kept 72 hours and a recount had to be requested in writing within 48. If a majority of the council found an impropriety it held a new election, contested only by candidates already eligible. The codes adopted on 22 January 2004 reset the caps at $450 for president, $400 for executive vice president, $350 for the other cabinet offices and $50 for legislative seats, shortened appeals to three business days, and moved voting to internet polling on 16 and 17 March 2004.

Three rosters survive. In 2000-01 Nathan Hopper was chief justice with Adrienne Frey, Heidi Grogg, Joe Morell and Brandon Copeland; SGA's website described the five as reviewing legislation when Congress or the Executive Cabinet asked, overseeing the homecoming queen and executive elections, and interpreting the constitution on request. In 2001-02 Heidi Grogg was chief justice with Copeland, Robert Unseld Jr., Amanda Demarest and Mike Richardson. Holly Skidmore was chief justice in 2002-03 and made the spring 2003 general election results public shortly after 1 a.m. on the Friday, the poll having closed the previous night. By January 2004 the council was Chief Justice Troy Ransdell with Scott Broadbent, Josh Collins, Gretchen Light and Kristin Hartley, and the website told applicants that appointments needed the approval of Congress and that prior service in Congress was expected.

The Herald index for April 1999 lists an item on the Judicial Council questioning candidate Joe Matheis in the vice president of finance race, and another on 27 April on Ryan Morrison winning an SGA election. Those articles have not been read for this account, so no result, margin or ruling is stated here. The index also lists a report headed on confirmed election violations in the issue of 23 April 2002, likewise not read. Nothing else about the council between 1992-93 and 1999-2000 has been located in the sources consulted here.

The council's own code of conduct, dated 8 September 2003, set the order of a hearing: five minutes for the opening argument by the person requesting an interpretation, five for each rebuttal, then deliberation, then a verdict that did not have to be given at that meeting but had to appear in the minutes. It recorded a separation of powers rule under which no justice served on a congressional committee or authored legislation, and reserved the council's right to refuse a request for interpretation it deemed frivolous or unwarranted.

SGA's minutes archive listed six Judicial Council meetings for 2003-04, running from September to December 2003. Two of the six files survive. The first, of 8 September 2003, recorded four justices with the fifth seat still unfilled, the adoption of a code of conduct, and a tentative weekly meeting time. The second, of 6 October 2003, recorded attendance hearings for three Congress members who did not appear to defend themselves and a decision to remove them. SGA's index page dates that meeting 10 October, while the file and its own heading give 6 October.

The constitution proposed in fall 2003 kept the Judicial Council at five justices appointed by the president with a two-thirds vote of what was now the Senate, and extended judicial review from the acts of Congress alone to the actions of both the Executive Cabinet and the Senate. It required the council to meet no less than twice a month, barred justices from membership in any other branch, and gave the council discretion over the timeline, applications and campaigning for the special election that KRS 164.321 required when the student regent seat fell vacant. Impeachment in every case needed the written endorsement of a fifth of the Senate, a wait of fourteen days, and a two-thirds vote of the full Senate sitting as a judicial body, with the chief justice presiding except when a justice was in the dock, when the Speaker did. The bylaws adopted with it added a power of censure: a request from ten or more people against any executive or legislative officer was investigated by the council, which issued a censure if it found the officer neglecting or wanting in their duties, while a request against a justice went to the other four with the president presiding and breaking ties. Senators were allowed four absences a semester unless the council excused them.

The council's reach was written into the constitution itself in spring 2002, when voters passed the Supremacy Clause amendment, making the constitution the supreme law of the association and putting every ruling and enactment under it, subject to federal, state and university law, and making it the duty of Congress members, executive officers and justices alike to know its contents.
problems:
The summary is not publishable. The governing-document paragraphs are largely sound; the narrative paragraphs are the problem, and almost every number in the last two paragraphs comes from nowhere in the fact list.

Numbers, dates and counts the facts do not carry:
1. "Ryan Morrison won the re-run on 26 April 1999 by 346 votes to 99." No cited fact mentions a re-run, a date or a margin. Nothing in this repository does either. What exists is a headline in the Herald index for 27 April 1999, "Ryan Morrison Wins Student Government Association Election", and the article behind it has not been read. This is the exact failure the brief warns about: a headline treated as the article, with two invented-looking figures attached.
2. "After reviewing Joe Matheis's campaign fliers ... the council let the result stand, then voided it." The repository's own 1998-99 entries say the council reviewed and let the result stand, and that a later Herald issue reported the election overturned. Whether the same race was voided, and on whose motion, is not established by any cited fact.
3. "On 6 October 2003 it removed three Congress members." This one is true. I opened the surviving minutes and they record attendance hearings for three named members who did not appear and a decision to remove them. But no numbered fact carries it, so as written the page asserts it with no citation. It also conflicts with SGA's own index label of October 10 for that meeting.
4. "In late January and early February 2004 it struck about thirteen more from the roll, which gave Congress the two-thirds attendance needed to pass a new constitution at the fifth attempt on 10 February." Nothing in the fact list supports any part of this: not the thirteen, not the fifth attempt, not 10 February, and not the causal link. Fact 19 establishes that no Judicial Council minutes survive past 1 December 2003, so the stated source of this paragraph does not exist.
5. "Students ratified it on 9 March 2004, 116 votes to 16 of 132 cast." The 116 and the 16 are unsourced. The only figure in the record is that 132 of about 18,000 students voted, from a Herald editorial. The 9 March date appears in one cited source only, the 2004 Election Codes calendar, where it is marked tentative.
6. "In April 2004 the council ruled a two-week impeachment of the president-elect could not finish before he left the office in question." Not carried by any cited fact.

Continuity implied where the archive has no record:
7. The whole opening is written flat for 1992-93 through 2003-04, but the only constitution read is the spring 2001 text. Five justices, the one-year term, the 2.5 grade point average and the two-week rules are evidenced from 2001 and 2004 only; for 1992 through 2000 the sole evidence is Bill 93-1-F, which shows the council existed and that appointments took a majority vote.
8. "The council met at least twice a month" is the spring 2002 bylaws and the 2004 constitution. The 2001 constitution instead has the chief justice schedule bi-weekly meetings. Stated flat, it claims a rule for a decade on the strength of two years.
9. "It could exempt an executive candidate from the requirement of a year's prior membership" is presented as standing throughout, when Amendment 4, printed on the same page as the fact that sources it, set service requirements and said no exemptions were to be made.

Claims attributed to the wrong document:
10. "The constitution ... gave it supervision of all elections." The supervision language is the opening line of the 2000 Election Codes, which cite Article IV, Section 5. The archived constitution's judicial article does not contain it; it gives the council appeals, election rules and election committees.
11. "If a majority of the council found an impropriety, it held a new election. It did that in April 1999." The codes quoted are dated 7 March 2000, a year after the event. A 1999 action cannot be an application of them.
12. "From September 2003 the council's own minutes survive" over-reads fact 19. Two sets survive out of six meetings listed; the other four links are dead.

Sourcing and living-people problems:
13. "The Herald recorded confirmed election violations again in April 2002" rests on a headline, "Election Violations Confirmed", in the 23 April 2002 issue. No article has been read, no fact cites it, and the sentence states no who, what or outcome. Under this repository's rule on living people, an unread violations headline should not be published as a finding at all.
14. The April 2004 impeachment sentence concerns a living person and gives an allegation-adjacent process with no outcome. The record in this repository is that the president-elect denied wrongdoing publicly and was sworn in with the investigation unresolved. If the sentence stays, the outcome must stay with it.
15. "The archive holds little other judicial business before 2003" is an unsourced characterisation of an absence. Say what has been searched, not what does not exist.

Smaller matters worth fixing while you are in there: the 2000 caps are presented as the routine with no mention that the codes adopted on 22 January 2004 replaced them and moved voting online; judicial review is described without the condition that a registered student had to request it; and Dana Lockhart, carried in fact 16 as an associate justice, should not appear at all until the 6 February 2003 Herald citation is produced with a working URL.

What I could not establish, honestly:

1. THE 1990s ARE NEARLY BLANK FOR THIS BRANCH. Between 1992-93 and 1997-98 I found no record of a single Judicial Council meeting, ruling, roster or chief justice. The complete Herald index (data/herald-index-full.json, 17,601 index lines) contains exactly one headline naming the Judicial Council between 1988 and 2005: 13 April 1999. The SGA collection on TopSCHOLAR has no judicial series. The record is silent; I have not written around it. What survives for those years is the constitution's text and two Herald headlines (a candidate warned over campaign policy in April 1994, ballot amendments in April 1996).

2. NO JUDICIAL COUNCIL ROSTER exists in any source I found for 1992-93 through 1999-2000. The first roster I could source is 2000-01. For 1999-2000 the archive names only chief justice John Crowe and member Drew Harvill, and that is already in years.json from the Herald.

3. THE 1999 VOIDING IS THIN ON PROCESS. The Herald issues of 6, 13, 15, 20 and 27 April 1999 are image-scanned PDFs on TopSCHOLAR with no text layer, so I could not read beyond what a previous pass had already transcribed into years.json. I could not establish the vote by which the council voided the race, who sat on the council besides Crowe and Harvill, or whether the separate SGA investigation into racially charged fliers naming Will Jones was ever resolved. No source I found reports an outcome to that investigation.

4. APRIL 2002 "ELECTION VIOLATIONS CONFIRMED" is a headline and nothing more. wkuherald.com's full text does not reach back before August 2002 (I checked: the WordPress API returns nothing for spring 2002), and the TopSCHOLAR issue is an index listing. Which candidate, which rule and what the council did are unknown.

5. FOUR OF THE SIX 2003-04 JUDICIAL COUNCIL MINUTES ARE LOST. SGA's own index lists meetings on 22 September, October, 3 November, 17 November and 1 December 2003, but only 8 September and 6 October were captured by the Wayback Machine. There is also a discrepancy I did not resolve: the 8 September minutes list a "Justice Scott Jaggers" where the 6 October minutes and the profiles page have Justice Scott Broadbent. I have not merged them.

6. A CORRECTION THE EDITOR SHOULD SEE. years.json (event dated 2004-01-01, sourced to wku.edu/sga/about/history.php) says the 2004 Constitutional Convention created "three branches drawn from the student body at large" and that "every enrolled student became a member of SGA with the right to vote in its elections." Both clauses were already in the constitution as amended in spring 2001, which I read in full (https://web.archive.org/web/20040106170252/http://www.wku.edu:80/Dept/Org/Student/SGA/constitution.html). Its opening article names three branches and makes all enrolled students members with the right to vote in all SGA elections. The 2004 document renamed Congress the Senate, cut it from 75 seats to 35, required senators to be elected, extended judicial review to the Executive Cabinet as well as the legislature, and added a censure power. It did not create the three-branch structure. The archive's own SGA history page is a later compilation and should not outrank the constitution text.

The fact that Ryan Morrison won the re-run on 26 April 1999 by 346 to 99 is in years.json, but only inside the 1999-00 organization block as a note on the vice president of finance, not as a dated event. I have marked it already_in_archive so it is not duplicated, but the editor may want it as an event in its own right.

Its PDF returned HTTP 202 with an empty body on two attempts 95 seconds apart, so I did not read it and have claimed nothing about its contents.
